source_refs.note: Book p. 50-51: 4.2.4 Multiplication of two Matrices: conformability, the 2x3 by 3x2 product with Figure (A), AB (i) and BA (ii), Note 1, Note 2 with its order diagram, Example 2 (A^2 B) and the Note on powers of square matrices. Teaching notes, our worked illustration, the extra steps of the...

blocks.text: Two matrices \(A\) and \(B\) are said to be conformable for the product \(AB\) if the number of columns of \(A\) is equal to the number of rows of \(B\).

Let \(A = [a_{ij}]\) be a \(2 \times 3\) matrix and \(B = [b_{ij}]\) be a \(3 \times 2\) matrix. Then the product \(AB\) is defined to be the \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(C\) whose element \(c_{ij}\) is the sum of the products of the corresponding elements of the \(i\)th row of \(A\) with the elements of the \(j\)th column of \(B\). For example, the element \(c_{21}\) of \(C\) is shown in figure (A), that is

blocks.alt: Labelled 2nd row of A: the entries a21, a22, a23 across the bottom. Bent arrows (magenta, cyan, magenta) go up from a21, a22 and a23 and across to b11, b21 and b31, written one below the other on the right under the heading 1st column of B.
blocks.caption: Figure (A): the 2nd row of A meets the 1st column of B to give c21 (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why row by column? Each row of \(A\) has 3 entries and each column of \(B\) has 3 entries, so they can be paired off: first with first, second with second, third with third. Multiply each pair and add. That is why the number of columns of \(A\) must equal the number of rows of \(B\): otherwise some entry would be left without a partner.
To find \(c_{ij}\), put one finger on row \(i\) of \(A\) and another on column \(j\) of \(B\), and move both together. (In the scan the labels of figure (A) are hard to read; the pairs are \(a_{21}\) with \(b_{11}\), \(a_{22}\) with \(b_{21}\), \(a_{23}\) with \(b_{31}\).)
From (i) and (ii), \(AB\) and \(BA\) are both calculated; their orders are \(2 \times 2\) and \(3 \times 3\) respectively.

blocks.title: Note 2
blocks.text: If the product \(AB\) is defined, then the order of the product can be illustrated as given below: order of \(A\) is \(m \times n\), order of \(B\) is \(n \times p\), order of \(AB\) is \(m \times p\).

blocks.alt: Three lines: Order of A, m × n; Order of B, n × p; Order of AB, m × p, each order in a pale blue box. A curved arrow on the left goes from m in the order of A to m in the order of AB; a curved arrow on the right goes from p in the order of B to p in the order of AB.
blocks.caption: Figure: Note 2, the order of the product AB (original drawing after the textbook's diagram)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Our example (not from the book), with \(C = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}\) and \(D = \begin{bmatrix}5 & 6 \\ 7 & 8\end{bmatrix}\):
\[c_{11} = (1)(5) + (2)(7) = 19\]
\[c_{12} = (1)(6) + (2)(8) = 22\]
\[c_{21} = (3)(5) + (4)(7) = 43\]
\[c_{22} = (3)(6) + (4)(8) = 50\]
\[CD = \begin{bmatrix}19 & 22 \\ 43 & 50\end{bmatrix}\]
In the other order
\[DC = \begin{bmatrix}23 & 34 \\ 31 & 46\end{bmatrix}\]
Both products exist, yet \(CD \ne DC\): Note 1 in action. With matrices the order of the factors matters, unlike with numbers.

blocks.title: Example 2
steps:
Given: \(A\) and \(B\), both \(3 \times 3\).
To find: \(A^{2}B\).
Method: \(A^{2}\) means \(A \cdot A\) (not the squares of the entries). First find \(A^{2} = A \cdot A\), then multiply it by \(B\). Every entry comes from the row-by-column rule. Orders: \(3 \times 3\) times \(3 \times 3\); the inner 3's match, so each product is defined and is again \(3 \times 3\).

Step 1: First row of \(A^{2} = A \cdot A\) (\(p_{ij}\) = entries of \(A^{2}\))
\[p_{11} = (2)(2) + (-1)(1) + (0)(1) = 3\]
\[p_{12} = (2)(-1) + (-1)(2) + (0)(2) = -4\]
\[p_{13} = (2)(0) + (-1)(-3) + (0)(-2) = 3\]
Why: row 1 of \(A\) is matched with each column of \(A\): first entry times first, second times second, third times third, then add.

Step 2: Second row of \(A^{2} = A \cdot A\) (\(p_{ij}\) = entries of \(A^{2}\))
\[p_{21} = (1)(2) + (2)(1) + (-3)(1) = 1\]
\[p_{22} = (1)(-1) + (2)(2) + (-3)(2) = -3\]
\[p_{23} = (1)(0) + (2)(-3) + (-3)(-2) = 0\]
Why: row 2 of \(A\) is matched with each column of \(A\): first entry times first, second times second, third times third, then add.

Step 3: Third row of \(A^{2} = A \cdot A\) (\(p_{ij}\) = entries of \(A^{2}\))
\[p_{31} = (1)(2) + (2)(1) + (-2)(1) = 2\]
\[p_{32} = (1)(-1) + (2)(2) + (-2)(2) = -1\]
\[p_{33} = (1)(0) + (2)(-3) + (-2)(-2) = -2\]
Why: row 3 of \(A\) is matched with each column of \(A\): first entry times first, second times second, third times third, then add.

Step 4: Write \(A^{2}\)
\[A^{2} = \begin{bmatrix}3 & -4 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & -2\end{bmatrix}\]
Why: the nine entries above are placed in their positions.

Step 5: First row of \(A^{2}B\) (\(q_{ij}\) = entries of \(A^{2}B\))
\[q_{11} = (3)(2) + (-4)(-1) + (3)(0) = 10\]
\[q_{12} = (3)(-2) + (-4)(-4) + (3)(-5) = -5\]
\[q_{13} = (3)(3) + (-4)(6) + (3)(5) = 0\]
Why: row 1 of \(A^{2}\) is matched with each column of \(B\). Negative numbers are kept in brackets to avoid sign slips.

Step 6: Second row of \(A^{2}B\) (\(q_{ij}\) = entries of \(A^{2}B\))
\[q_{21} = (1)(2) + (-3)(-1) + (0)(0) = 5\]
\[q_{22} = (1)(-2) + (-3)(-4) + (0)(-5) = 10\]
\[q_{23} = (1)(3) + (-3)(6) + (0)(5) = -15\]
Why: row 2 of \(A^{2}\) is matched with each column of \(B\). Negative numbers are kept in brackets to avoid sign slips.

Step 7: Third row of \(A^{2}B\) (\(q_{ij}\) = entries of \(A^{2}B\))
\[q_{31} = (2)(2) + (-1)(-1) + (-2)(0) = 5\]
\[q_{32} = (2)(-2) + (-1)(-4) + (-2)(-5) = 10\]
\[q_{33} = (2)(3) + (-1)(6) + (-2)(5) = -10\]
Why: row 3 of \(A^{2}\) is matched with each column of \(B\). Negative numbers are kept in brackets to avoid sign slips.

Check: one entry by another route. \(A^{2}B\) also equals \(A(AB)\) (associative property, 4.3). The first column of \(AB\) is \(2(2) + (-1)(-1) + 0(0) = 5\), \(1(2) + 2(-1) + (-3)(0) = 0\), \(1(2) + 2(-1) + (-2)(0) = 0\). Then the first row of \(A\) times this column: \(2(5) + (-1)(0) + 0(0) = 10\), which agrees with \(q_{11} = 10\).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Powers of square matrices are defined as: \(A^{2} = A \times A\), \(A^{3} = A \times A \times A\), \(A^{n} = A \times A \times A \times \cdots\) to \(n\) factors.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Powers exist only for square matrices: for \(A \cdot A\) to be defined, the columns of \(A\) must equal the rows of \(A\). And \(A^{2}\) is never found by squaring each entry: for \(C = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{bmatrix}\), \(C^{2} = \begin{bmatrix}7 & 10 \\ 15 & 22\end{bmatrix}\), not \(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 \\ 9 & 16 \end{bmatrix}\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(AB\) is defined only when (columns of \(A\)) = (rows of \(B\)).
2. \(c_{ij}\) = row \(i\) of \(A\) times column \(j\) of \(B\): multiply pairs and add.
3. Order rule: \((m \times n)(n \times p) = m \times p\).
4. In general \(AB \ne BA\); one of them may even be undefined.
5. \(A^{n} = A \cdot A \cdots A\) (\(n\) factors), only for square \(A\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Multiplying entry by entry (\(a_{ij}b_{ij}\)) as in addition. Matrix multiplication is row by column.
2. Using a column of \(A\) or a row of \(B\).
3. Assuming \(AB = BA\) and changing the order of factors.
4. Writing \(A^{2}\) as the squares of the entries.
5. Sign slips with negative entries: keep them in brackets, \((-1)(-4) = 4\).
